summary: This overview synthesizes 9 sources covering the full landscape of automated trading strategies on Polymarket prediction markets, with particular focus on crypto UP/DOWN short-duration contracts (5-min and 15-min BTC/ETH). The strategies range from pure-speed latency arbitrage (exploiting the 2-12 second repricing lag between Binance and Polymarket) to non-directional market making and liquidity capture systems. The central case study is the 0x8dxd wallet that turned $313 into $2.38M over 4 months using latency arbitrage with 98% win rate across 26,738 trades. Four distinct strategy categories emerge: latency arbitrage, oracle arbitrage, news-driven trading, and market making. All profitable systems share common infrastructure requirements (sub-50ms data feeds, CLOB API integration, Kelly-based sizing) and risk management primitives (kill switches, position caps, drawdown limits). The sources collectively argue that non-predictive, structurally-exploitative approaches dominate predictive/directional ones, and that the primary differentiator between success and failure is risk management quality rather than strategy sophistication.

concepts.name: Latency Arbitrage (CEX-to-Prediction-Market)
concepts.description: Exploits the structural lag between centralized exchange (CEX) price movements and prediction market contract repricing. The bot monitors real-time BTC/ETH price feeds from Binance via WebSocket and executes on Polymarket's CLOB at stale odds before the market catches up. This is the highest-performing strategy documented, with the 0x8dxd wallet achieving $313 to $2.38M in 4 months.
key_details: Repricing lag was ~12+ seconds in 2024, compressed to ~2.7 seconds by Q1 2026 due to competition
Bot monitors Binance WebSocket with sub-50ms latency
Edge threshold typically 3-5% divergence between CEX-implied probability and Polymarket odds
Example: BTC drops 0.6% on Binance, 'Down' should be ~78%, Polymarket still shows 54% -- bot buys at 54 cents
Win rate: 85-98% because the bot reads confirmed price action, not predictions
0x8dxd: 26,738 trades, 98% win rate, $4-5K per trade, consistent sizing
200-500 trades per day typical execution frequency
Existential risk: window compression makes strategy uneconomical for retail as more bots enter
Requires sub-50ms data ingestion and fast CLOB API execution to remain competitive

concepts.name: Stoikov Market Making Model
concepts.description: A quantitative quote-placement and inventory-risk management model used by high-frequency market-making bots. The Stoikov pricing rule determines optimal bid/ask placement by accounting for inventory risk, time remaining, and volatility. Formula: r = s - q * gamma * sigma^2 * (T - t), where r is the reservation price adjustment, s is the mid-price, q is inventory, gamma is risk aversion, sigma is volatility, and T-t is time to expiry.
key_details: Handles quote placement and inventory risk simultaneously
Adjusts reservation price based on current inventory position to avoid accumulating directional risk
Combined with Bayesian probability updates in the documented HF bot
The HF bot using Stoikov achieved $157K deposit to $1.03M PnL (+654% ROI) in 2 months
Operates on short crypto UP/DOWN markets with rapid turnover
Recycling small edges across many positions with YES + NO < 100 cents

concepts.name: Bayesian Probability Updating
concepts.description: Using Bayes' theorem P(H|D) = P(D|H) * P(H) / P(D) to continuously update the bot's internal probability estimate before the market has fully repriced the odds. This gives the bot an informational edge during the brief window between new data arriving and the market reflecting it.
key_details: Updates the bot's internal probability in real-time as new price data arrives
Creates an edge during the repricing window -- bot knows the 'true' probability before the market does
Part of the HF market-making system that achieved +654% ROI
Also used in the multi-strategy bot for continuous probability updates during execution
Works on the principle that prior beliefs are updated with each new data point (price tick, news event)

concepts.name: Kelly Criterion Position Sizing
concepts.description: A mathematical formula for optimal bet sizing: f = (bp - q) / b, where f is the fraction of capital to wager, b is the odds received, p is the probability of winning, and q is the probability of losing. Used across multiple strategies to determine how large each position should be relative to the portfolio, maximizing long-term growth rate while controlling ruin risk.
key_details: Fractional Kelly (e.g., half-Kelly) commonly used to reduce variance at cost of slightly lower growth
0x8dxd bot used fractional Kelly sizing -- not full Kelly
Maximum single position size capped at 8% of total portfolio as additional safeguard
Sizes positions proportionally to edge: larger edge = larger position (unlike human emotional sizing)
The key differentiator between the successful Claude bot (+1,322%) and the liquidated OpenClaw bot in the March 2026 comparison
Multi-strategy bot uses 'capped Kelly' -- Kelly output is capped at a maximum percentage
Critical that every trade passes minimum edge thresholds before Kelly is applied

concepts.name: Market Making (Spread Capture)
concepts.description: A non-directional strategy where the bot places simultaneous buy and sell orders on both sides of a prediction market, earning the bid-ask spread on every matched trade. No outcome prediction is required -- the bot provides liquidity and profits from the spread between YES and NO sides. The most consistent and hardest-to-blow-up strategy, returning 2-5% per month on deployed capital.
key_details: Bot places ladders of bids at multiple price levels (typically 1-cent increments) on both UP and DOWN sides
Profit source: capturing spread when other participants cross the spread, not predicting direction
Risk: inventory accumulation if market moves sharply in one direction before unwinding
Best run on high-liquidity markets where spread is wide enough to justify inventory risk
Strict inventory limits prevent directional exposure from accumulating
Returns 2-5% monthly on deployed capital, compounding aggressively
Transforms the bot from a trader into 'infrastructure' within the market
Requires substantial capital for a wide ladder with meaningful order sizes

concepts.name: Bid Ladder Architecture
concepts.description: The order placement pattern used by market-making bots: placing a ladder of bids at multiple price levels, typically in 1-cent increments, across both YES and NO sides of a prediction market. As price moves through these levels, orders get filled sequentially, creating the structural imbalance that generates profit.
key_details: Orders placed at 1-cent increments across the price range
Both YES and NO sides have simultaneous ladders
As price trends in one direction, the bot accumulates more positions on the winning side
Naive flat ladders underperform -- successful bots use non-linear (weighted/curved) distributions
Ladder Larry bot: aggressive HF laddering approach, +$12,450 in 24h
Width and density of the ladder depends on available capital and market liquidity
Orders at each level compete for fills via FIFO queue priority

concepts.name: Non-Linear Order Distribution
concepts.description: The practice of allocating order sizes across a bid ladder using a curved or weighted function rather than equal sizing at every level. More size is allocated to price levels where fills are more likely, and less size to extreme levels. This is described as the most important and least understood aspect of liquidity capture strategies.
key_details: Flat/equal distribution across ladder levels gets 'eaten alive' by sophisticated competitors
Optimal shape resembles a curved function centered around the current price
Requires repeated live testing to calibrate -- depends on market behavior, volatility, and participant flow

concepts.name: Position Merging / Capital Recycling
concepts.description: On Polymarket, holding both YES and NO shares allows combining them into a guaranteed payout of $1. Merging opposing positions is used to remove exposure and recycle capital back into the system. Most merges occur at a slight loss, but this is intentional -- merging is a capital-efficiency mechanism, not a profit center.
key_details: Holding YES + NO = guaranteed $1 payout (pair-sum arbitrage)
Merges often result in small losses, which is by design
Purpose: eliminate losing inventory and free capital for new orders
Enables continuous operation without accumulating excessive directional risk
Merge Phantom bot specialized in this: +$9,830 in 24h through capital recycling
Critical for long-running market-making strategies that would otherwise lock up capital in opposing positions

concepts.name: Structural Imbalance Profit Mechanism
concepts.description: The core profit mechanism of non-directional market making: when price trends in one direction, a bot with laddered bids on both sides naturally accumulates more positions on the winning side than the losing side. This happens mechanically through how price moves through discrete bid levels, not through prediction.
key_details: If market trends upward, bot fills more bids on the UP side (price moves through those levels)
DOWN side orders receive fewer fills because price moves away from them
Creates a natural long bias on the correct side without any directional intent
Not based on prediction -- purely a mechanical consequence of laddered order placement
Over many iterations, this imbalance becomes the primary source of profit
Works because the bot is 'structurally owning the platform' rather than trading it

concepts.name: Structural Edge Detection
concepts.description: Using AI to identify structural mispricings in prediction markets by comparing market-implied probabilities against external data, historical base rates, and cross-market consistency rather than trying to predict outcomes. Cross-market: related contracts on same event can be internally inconsistent (e.g., candidate weak in state but strong nationally)
Mechanical moves: distinguishing real information moves from thin-orderbook noise
Certainty overpricing: crowds overpay for high-confidence outcomes and underpay for uncertainty
Time pressure: markets stay too expensive as calendar narrows remaining possibilities

The strategy exploits the 2-12 second repricing lag between Binance price movements and Polymarket contract odds updates.

Four distinct strategy categories dominate Polymarket bot trading: latency arbitrage (85-98% win rate), oracle arbitrage (78-85%), news-driven trading (60-75%), and market making (2-5%/month steady returns). Each has different risk profiles, capital requirements, and durability characteristics.

Non-directional strategies consistently outperform directional prediction. Building 1,000+ bots confirmed that almost all failures came from trying to predict outcomes rather than structurally extracting edge from market mechanics. Risk management quality is the single most important differentiator between success and failure. The March 2026 Claude vs OpenClaw comparison proved this: identical strategy, identical starting capital, but Claude's code produced +1,322% return while OpenClaw was liquidated due to inferior position sizing and missing drawdown protection.

The latency arbitrage window is compressing irreversibly: from 12+ seconds in 2024 to ~2.7 seconds by Q1 2026. At some point it will be smaller than round-trip API latency for retail operators, making the strategy uneconomical without co-located infrastructure. This makes latency arbitrage a time-limited business.

Non-linear order distribution is the key differentiator among market-making bots. In a 24-hour competition between three liquidity capture bots, the Curve Alchemist (non-linear curves, +$18,920) outperformed Ladder Larry (flat HF laddering, +$12,450) and Merge Phantom (capital recycling focus, +$9,830). Simple copies with flat distributions fail to replicate results.

Position merging (combining YES+NO for $1 guaranteed payout) is not a profit mechanism but a critical capital recycling tool. Most merges occur at slight losses, but they free capital for new orders and prevent inventory accumulation from halting the system.

Claude's structural edge detection identifies six specific categories of crowd mispricing: narrative overreaction vs base rates, cross-market inconsistency, mechanical vs informational price moves, cross-platform discrepancies, certainty premium, and time decay underpricing. None require predicting outcomes.

Automated bots produce approximately 2x the returns of humans using the same strategy on the same market ($206K vs $100K documented), due to four systematic human disadvantages: late entries, inconsistent (emotional) sizing, fatigue, and drawdown psychology.

A multi-strategy bot combining spread farming, wallet copytrade, pump sniping, and news-edge trading achieved 73% win rate across 1,672 trades with Sharpe ratio 2.59 on its first day, built for $20 of Claude API usage. The multi-agent architecture uses progressive context loading to keep execution fast.

Infrastructure specifications are vague. While sub-50ms latency and Polygon RPC endpoints are mentioned, specific hosting requirements, co-location options, network optimization techniques, and cost structures for competitive latency arbitrage infrastructure are not covered.

Capital requirements for market making at scale are mentioned as 'substantial' but never quantified. What constitutes minimum viable capital for a ladder with meaningful order sizes on $50K+ liquidity markets is not specified.
